title: Everyone hates the "elites," but who are they?
gist: Discussing new polling from The Argument, Yglesias notes Americans define 'elites' primarily as the very rich and celebrities rather than intellectuals, argues the public underrates real influence-holders like Walmart CEO John Furner relative to mere billionaires, and highlights a broad elite-mass perception gap on health insurance, business ownership, free trade, and gender roles.

themes.theme: Who the public thinks 'the elite' actually is

insights.claim: New polling from The Argument found that when Americans are asked who 'the elites' are, they answer primarily 'the very rich,' followed by celebrities, and to a lesser extent business executives and elected officials.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Populist political messaging that targets 'the rich' rather than 'intellectuals' or 'the establishment' is better aligned with how the mass public actually defines elite status — relevant for reading which anti-elite rhetoric will resonate in 2026-28 campaigns.
insights.locator: 'This week, Jerusalem and I discuss interesting polling'

insights.claim: The mass public largely rejects the conservative concept of an 'intellectual elite' composed of professors, journalists, and people with advanced degrees, aligning instead with the left-populist idea that anti-elitism is basically just hostility to rich people.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Conservative anti-'expert class' messaging may have less mass-public traction than assumed; left-coded wealth-focused populism appears to better match how voters actually conceive of 'elites.'
insights.locator: 'The mass public largely rejects the conservative concept'

insights.claim: Yglesias suggests the 'celebrity' polling category may resolve the apparent tension between intellectual and wealth-based definitions of elite, since a sufficiently famous journalist or professor can shade into the 'celebrity' bucket and thereby register as elite in respondents' minds.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A methodological caution for interpreting elite-perception polling: category boundaries (celebrity vs. intellectual vs. wealthy) may blur in ways that understate how much the public still associates prominence/fame-driven visibility with elite status.
insights.locator: 'One point I raise is that the “celebrity” category'

insights.claim: Yglesias argues a famous journalist has more real social and political influence than a similarly famous actor, athlete, or musician, even though top entertainers are far more famous overall than the most famous journalists.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Distinguishes raw fame from actual policy/political influence — a useful lens for weighting media-figure commentary versus entertainer commentary in shaping public discourse.
insights.locator: 'if what you’re interested in is social and political influence'

insights.claim: Yglesias's strongest disagreement with the polled public is its overweighting of billionaire status relative to business-executive role as a marker of 'elite' status; he argues someone like Walmart CEO John Furner is a genuinely important actor in American society even with 'only' a low-nine-figure net worth.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Argues the meaningful 'elite' category for tracking real-world influence should be built around institutional power (Fortune 500 CEOs, regulators, senators) rather than net worth alone — relevant for anyone modeling which actors actually move policy or markets.

insights.claim: Walmart founder Sam Walton's grandson Lukas is far wealthier than Walmart's current CEO John Furner, but Yglesias argues Furner has more real-world influence because far more people care what he thinks and does in his operating role.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration that inherited wealth and operating-executive influence are not interchangeable — useful when assessing which family-wealth heirs versus which hired executives actually shape corporate/market outcomes.
insights.locator: 'Walmart founder Sam Walton’s grandson Lukas is a lot richer'

insights.claim: Yglesias states that senators and four-star generals and admirals are absolutely part of the American elite despite receiving relatively modest formal compensation, reinforcing his view that 'elite' status should track prestige and influence rather than wealth alone.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A definitional framework useful for any analysis distinguishing 'wealthy' from 'powerful' actors when assessing who actually shapes policy or institutional outcomes.

insights.claim: Voters perceive elites as disagreeing with them about nearly everything: most Americans believe in a government guarantee of health insurance, and most believe elites do not support this policy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A large perceived elite-mass gap on health-insurance guarantees signals continued political salience/vulnerability for any policymaker seen as opposing universal coverage guarantees, regardless of their actual position.
insights.locator: 'most people believe in a government guarantee of health insurance'

insights.claim: Most Americans oppose government ownership of most businesses, but a larger share of the public believes elites support that policy — another instance of a perceived elite-mass gap that doesn't match the substance of the debate.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Shows the public may overestimate elite support for nationalization/state-ownership policies that are actually fringe even among elites — relevant for gauging how 'socialism' attack lines land regardless of accuracy.
insights.locator: 'most people oppose government ownership of most businesses'

insights.claim: Polling shows Americans believe elites are against free trade and hold more traditional views about gender roles than the public itself does.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Suggests public perception of elite trade preferences may run counter to the actual pro-trade consensus among economic elites — a mismatch relevant to understanding trade-policy political economy and tariff politics.
insights.locator: 'Americans believe that elites are against free trade'
